title: Rethinking Entropy Allocation in LLM-based ASR: Understanding the Dynamics between Speech Encoders and Large Language Models
claim: Joint end-to-end training shifts encoder-side metrics substantially for one model pair but leaves them almost unchanged for another, revealing different entropy allocation.
layout: 2 groups of 3 bar panels (NSE, PAI, CSAI), before/after hatched vs solid bars
description: The figure has two side-by-side groups of bar charts. Each group has a large NSE panel (percent) on the left and two smaller stacked panels on the right, PAI (bits) on top and CSAI (bits) below. The left group compares FireRed encoder before end-to-end SFT (red hatched bars) and after (orange solid bars). NSE falls from 86.8 to 85.1, PAI falls from 23.50 to 21.60, and CSAI rises from 11.37 to 12.25. The right group compares the Whisper encoder before (blue hatched) and after (light blue solid), where the bars are nearly identical: NSE 90.2 vs 90.2, PAI 20.10 vs 20.05, CSAI 10.69 vs 10.68. Bold titles sit above each panel, with value labels on the bars and model-pair captions underneath. The eye goes first to the large NSE bars, then to the visible drop and rise in the FireRed panels.
caption: The shift in encoder-side metrics before and after joint training. We hold the encoder architecture fixed within each group to examine the impact of joint training on encoder representations.
abstract: Integrating large language models (LLMs) into automatic speech recognition (ASR) has become a dominant paradigm. Although recent LLM-based ASR models have shown promising performance on public benchmarks, it remains challenging to balance recognition quality with latency and overhead, while hallucinations further limit real-world deployment. In this study, we revisit LLM-based ASR from an entropy allocation perspective and introduce three metrics to characterize how training paradigms allocate entropy reduction between the speech encoder and the LLM. To remedy entropy-allocation inefficiencies in prevailing approaches, we propose a principled multi-stage training strategy grounded in capability-boundary awareness, optimizing parameter efficiency and hallucination robustness. Specifically, we redesign the pretraining strategy to alleviate the speech-text modality gap, and further introduce an iterative asynchronous SFT stage between alignment and joint SFT to preserve functional decoupling and constrain encoder representation drift. Experiments on Mandarin and English benchmarks show that our method achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art models using only 2.3B parameters, while also effectively mitigating hallucinations through our decoupling-oriented design.
